analysis.one_liner: Requires a federal license with safety training and a background check to buy any gun.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Judiciary Committee with one cosponsor until the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Rep. Andy Kim's bill would have made it illegal to buy or receive a firearm without a federal license. To get one, a person would need to pass a written gun-law test and a hands-on safety test, submit fingerprints, and clear a background check. It would also close the private-sale loophole by requiring all gun transfers, including sales between individuals, to go through a licensed dealer running a background check, and it would require private sellers to report every sale to the Attorney General.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people in communities affected by gun violence, if the licensing and universal background-check requirements reduce access to guns by people who are dangerous, as proponents of such laws argue.

how_it_helps.text: The bill makes it unlawful to purchase or receive a firearm without a valid federal license, and licenses require firearms-safety training with both a written test and hands-on firing tests, plus a background investigation, fingerprints, and proof of identity [S2].

It denies licenses to people prohibited by federal or state law and lets the Attorney General deny a license to someone who poses a significant danger of bodily injury, based on factors like threats or violence, domestic violence restraining orders, stalking, and drug or alcohol abuse, with judicial review of denials [S2].

It closes the private-sale loophole: unlicensed person-to-person gun transfers would be unlawful unless a licensed dealer first takes possession and runs the same background check used for dealer sales [S2].
It requires anyone who sells or transfers a gun to report the transaction, with identifying details, to the Attorney General within three business days, creating a record of private transfers [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers and sellers, who would face training, testing, fingerprinting, fees, and waiting periods; and the firearms industry, which would face a smaller and slower market.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, sellers, and the gun industry

drawbacks.text: Each license would be valid for the purchase of a single firearm and only for 30 days, so a buyer would need to repeat the application process for every gun, which would add time and cost even for law-abiding purchasers [S2].

State and local officials could submit information leading the Attorney General to deny a license based on factors like prior arrests without conviction or a history of drug or alcohol abuse, which critics of such standards argue gives officials broad discretion over a constitutional right, though denials can be reviewed in federal court [S2].

The requirement that every private transfer run through a licensed dealer would add dealer fees and logistical burden to routine transactions like family transfers and sales between acquaintances [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would impose real burdens on every gun buyer — training, testing, fees, and a fresh application for each purchase — in exchange for a licensing-and-background-check system that gun-safety advocates credit with reducing gun deaths in states that have similar laws. The strongest fair criticism is the single-purchase, 30-day license design, which is stricter than most state licensing systems and would multiply paperwork for lawful owners. Whether the safety gains justify that friction is the honest trade-off at the center of the bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, which never took it up, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Kim of New Jersey introduced the Responsible Gun Ownership Licensing Act on November 1, 2023 [S1][S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary the same day and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote [S4].
It drew one cosponsor, a Democrat, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill advancing [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun owners, sellers, and the firearms industry, which will not face a federal license requirement for gun purchases or a mandate that all private sales run through licensed dealers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun owners and the firearms industry

sides.party_line_note: Both the sponsor and the sole cosponsor were Democrats, and no Republican support appears in the record.

industries.note: The bill would make every private gun transfer run through a licensed dealer for a background check, making dealers the mandatory paid gateway for all secondhand sales. Gun-trade groups have historically opposed such mandates, even though this bill routes more business through dealers.
A licensing requirement with safety training, a per-gun license, and universal background checks would slow and shrink the retail market for firearms, reducing manufacturer sales.
